paper_title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on many reasoning benchmarks, yet growing evidence suggests that high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily imply robust reasoning ability (Song et al., 2026). single accuracy number on static test set conflates many things: language understanding, memorization, shortcut exploitation, and genuine reasoning. It tells us little about what model can actually do. 1 Recent work has made this conflation increasingly hard to ignore. Benchmarks designed to test logical reasoning can reward other strategies: Chung et al. (2025) report higher GPT-3.5 scores on ReClor and LogiQA2 when the prompt asks it to avoid logical reasoning, illustrating that accuracy alone need not diagnose the intended competence. Models that appear to reason well on standard test sets show systematic drops under controlled perturbations (Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Sanyal et al., 2022), and reasoning models can collapse as complexity grows (Lin et al., 2025; Shojaee et al., 2025). The natural reading is that reasoning is brittle, but this conflates two questions: whether the model fails to derive conclusion from fixed problem representation, or constructs different representation in the first place. Measuring performance on fixed test set is insufficient to tell these apart, and therefore insufficient to characterize models reasoning capability. We argue for different evaluation paradigm: competence-based evaluation. Drawing on Chomskys distinction between knowledge of language and its use (Chomsky, 1965), we adapt the competence/performance distinction to reasoning: underlying task knowledge and observed behavior on specific instances. CBE tests reliable application of that knowledge through an explicit behavioral condition. We also draw on the cognitive-science account given by Stenning and van Lambalgen (2008) for human reasoning, which distinguishes reasoning to an interpretation, establishing problems representation and the logic governing it, from reasoning from an interpretation, deriving conclusions within that form. This motivates separating the tasks latent structure from its realization in language. competence claim concerns the family of problems governed by the same rule, including larger instances and equivalent formulations. Exhaustively enumerating that family is infeasible. Concretely, instead of measuring accuracy on fixed test set, we define parameterized problem generator for target reasoning competence and test necessary behavioral condition: the model must answer correctly across the generated instances and their answer-preserving presentations. The evaluation target is problem family whose complexity can grow while the required competence remains the same. The generator exposes the assumptions of that family and permits evaluation at new scales under the same criterion. finite experiment can expose violations of the condition; success supports only the evaluated coverage. CBE characterizes the models competence boundary, the region in the generators parameter space where correct, invariant behavior deteriorates and exposes biases that aggregate accuracy can conceal. By holding logical form fixed and varying surface form across matched presentations, the evaluation produces competence profile rather than single score. Paired outputs reveal whether correct answers survive equivalent formulations. They do not by themselves locate failure in either internal reasoning stage. This approach yields several advantages at once. Fresh generation reduces dependence on particular published test items, although familiarity with the generator or learned shortcuts remains possible. It produces richer diagnostics than single accuracy number: the competence profile reveals where model fails and under which conditions, including problem size, distractors, and equivalent reformulations. Additionally, as models improve, the evaluation naturally extends by pushing the parameter range further, rather than requiring an entirely new benchmark. Existing generators and consistency tests supply important precedents (2); CBE makes the target competence, its family, and its correctness condition explicit within one evaluation design. We instantiate the competence-based evaluation framework on ordering tasks, fundamental reasoning primitive involving transitivity and comparison. Ordering is well suited as first instantiation: the ordering rule is unchanged for any finite number of entities, so an extremely simple task supports scalable problem family. The generator controls the latent order and renders matched presentations that vary premise order, converse phrasing, names order, and relation vocabulary (Figure 1). Failure on this elementary family violates the specified competence condition. Chain length scales input and presentation load; endpoint queries admit shortcut and do not isolate multistep inference (4.1). Appendix illustrates adoption of the framework by Horn-clause inference. Our results show why the distinction between performance and competence matters. Even strong models fail the CBE condition across the tested ordering family, while performing reasonably well over bounded complexity ranges. On front/behind at = 1024, GPT-4.1 retains 77.5% originalprompt accuracy but answers both matched presentations correctly on only 56.8% of valid pairs. Vocabulary changes alter model rankings. Chainof-thought extends strong performance, and GRPO improves held-out transfer, but the tested interventions leave substantial failures. Improved scores can therefore reflect an expanded range of successful performance without demonstrating competence across the family. Contributions. (1) Competence-based evaluation as general framework. We formalize the shift from performance on selected instances to competence condition on specified problem family, through parameterized task generator, presentation set, model, correctness criterion, and competence condition (3). (2) The CBE Ordering Benchmark. We instantiate the framework on an elementary ordering task with precisely controlled latent structure and matched presentations. Its size parameter extends the evaluation while retaining the same ordering rule (4). (3) multidimensional competence analysis. We evaluate six base models and reasoning/training interventions, showing where correctness fails under complexity and presentation changes (56). The analysis distinguishes gains in aggregate performance from gains in the range of correct, invariant behavior, and provides diagnostic evidence that can guide future model development.

sections.content: We position CBE relative to fixed test sets, generated complexity evaluations, and invariance tests. The distinction is the evaluation target: defined competence over scalable problem family, with correctness required across equivalent presentations. Appendix compares the designs by axis.

ReClor, LogiQA, AR-LSAT, and FOLIO assess reasoning on curated or annotated problems (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2022; Han et al., 2024a). DivLogicEval uses counterintuitive content to reduce shortcuts (Chung et al., 2025), while BIG-bench logical_deduction generates linear-ordering problems at several sizes (Srivastava et al., 2023). These datasets provide valuable samples of task performance. CBE organizes correctness across equivalent presentations and sizes around an explicit competence condition on specified problem family.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.content: RuleTaker, ProofWriter, CLUTRR, and PrOntoQA generate deductive or relational instances with controlled structure or depth (Clark et al., 2020; Tafjord et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2019; Saparov and He, 2023). DyVal, functional benchmarks, NPHardEval, and ZebraLogic likewise generate instances or vary complexity (Zhu et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025). ReCogLab is especially close: it generates relational reasoning, including transitive comparison, with entity count, reasoning length, and textual features as parameters (Liu et al., 2025). These works establish generation and complexity scaling as useful evaluation tools. CBE couples that control to an explicit competence condition on matched presentations and evaluates the resulting profile across the family. 2.

sections.title: 7 Discussion and Diagnostic Evidence
sections.content: The competence profile distinguishes correct answers across presentations from agreement on an incorrect default. higher aggregate score can reflect wider successful range while substantial failures persist elsewhere in the family. The chainof-thought and training studies illustrate this distinction. Open-weight interventions provide supporting evidence. In Qwen3-8B, ablating selected heads raises invariance from 81.0% to 93.0% while original/equivalent accuracy falls from 64.5/59.5% to 59.0/52.0%. Stable answers can therefore accompany reduced task signal. In Qwen3.5-9B, shortchain answers remain linearly decodable despite biased outputs; longer-chain equivalents show reduced decodability at measured layer and position. GRPO strengthens the measured signal relative to the answer default. These results characterize possible contributors without establishing complete mechanism. Appendix reports the probes and interventions. CBE turns such observations into reusable testing strategy: state the competence, specify family with controlled complexity, certify answerpreserving presentations, and report where correctness survives those changes. This makes model comparisons and intervention gains interpretable in terms of the behavior they actually support.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We proposed competence-based evaluation as methodology for evaluating LLM reasoning through problem family. Its five components make the target competence and its necessary behavioral condition explicit. The ordering instantiation tests reliable application of the same rule across growing inputs and equivalent presentations; it does not isolate an inference-depth limit. Even strong models fail that condition across the tested ordering family, despite reasonably good performance over bounded complexity ranges. Accuracy alone conceals additional deterioration and symmetric changes across equivalent presentations. Chain-of-thought extends successful performance, and GRPO improves held-out transfer under the tested recipes, but documented failures remain. Better performance therefore does not establish competence across the family. These profiles can guide model development by locating gains across sizes and presentations, while benchmark designers extend coverage under the same competence condition. The intended impact is an evaluation practice that grows with models: generate fresh instances, extend the complexity range, and test the same competence under matched presentations. CBE provides reusable way to distinguish an expanded range of success from demonstrated ability to handle the task throughout the evaluated family.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: CBE evaluates competence within specified problem family. Finite samples can reveal failures but cannot certify correctness throughout an unbounded family. Our ordering study and Hornclause adoption example leave broader reasoning competences untested. Extending CBE to richer tasks and wider presentation coverage would clarify how its diagnostic profiles generalize. Chain length measures input size and presentation load; endpoint queries admit shortcut. Our ordering results therefore do not isolate multistep inference capacity. Length and presentation changes are also not always separated. Future generators could independently control derivation depth, distracting information, and linguistic realization. Behavioral profiles and linear probes do not uniquely identify internal reasoning processes. Paired metrics also condition on valid answers, so agreement must be read alongside completion coverage. Broader sampling and causal interventions could connect systematic behavioral failures to their mechanisms. The reasoning and training interventions studied here leave many routes to improved competence unexplored. Their gains do not establish general ranking of training methods, particularly when data and budgets differ. Matched comparisons across training objectives, model families, and compute budgets would help identify which approaches extend correct, invariant behavior beyond the trained range.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: CBE is intended to support research on reasoning competence. potential societal risk is treating success on generated family as evidence of general reasoning ability or readiness for deployment in consequential settings. Conversely, failures on this family should not be taken as evidence that model lacks all useful reasoning abilities. We mitigate these interpretation risks by specifying the competence condition and evaluation coverage, reporting correctness alongside invariance, and keeping conclusions scoped to the tested family. Repeated optimization against known generator may also encourage benchmark-specific strategies; fresh instances alone do not establish transfer to other reasoning tasks. The reported ordering instances assign fictional relations to generic first-name labels or random strings, and gold answers are computed from the generated structure. These relations do not describe identifiable peoples actual attributes. No human participants or crowdworker annotations are used to establish the task labels. The English templates and name vocabulary do not constitute demographic or multilingual coverage. Although some templates concern attributes such as wealth or seniority, they should not be interpreted as claims about real people or population groups. Model inference, extended reasoning traces, and adapter training consume computational resources and energy. We reuse pretrained models and train LoRA adapters, but do not claim that these choices establish low environmental footprint. We report evaluation and training settings in Appendix B; aggregate energy consumption and carbon emissions were not measured. Reporting competence gains alongside their computational cost is an important direction for future evaluations.

For the POS relation, names are sampled without replacement from pool of about 2,500 first names; randomname control replaces them with random five-letter strings. For each instance the generator samples names a0, . . . , an1, emits the 1 adjacent comparisons ai ai+1 rendered in the relations forward phrase, and shuffles both the premise order and the names list independently of the chain. The query is the endpoint pair (a0, an1) with direction and gold answer balanced over the four cells. Prompt format. representative Protocol prompt at = 8, verbatim: There are 8 people standing in some order. Their names are [Heather, Charles, Joseph, James, Andrew, Michelle, Mark, Donna]. Their standing order can be described by the following set of rules: James is in front of Andrew. Joseph is in front of James. Mark is behind Donna. Heather is in front of Charles. Donna is in front of Joseph. Andrew is in front of Michelle. Charles is in front of Mark. Is Heather in front of Michelle? Provide your answer only as yes or no. Answer: The system prompt, identical for every model and for training, is You are helpful assistant. Answer logical reasoning questions concisely. Equivalent presentation under the two protocols. sections.title: Inference
sections.content: C.1 Mapping the Framework to New Task This appendix illustrates adoption of CBE beyond the ordering benchmark. The latent generator is Horn program over pronounceable pseudoword atoms. An exact forward-chaining oracle supplies the gold answer to goal-derivability query. The complexity parameter is the number of rules, {4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}. Positive programs derive the goal; negative near misses retain rule headed by the goal but sever its derivation at one point. Gold answers are balanced. Rule count indexes program size. Positive proof depth and distractor content co-vary with rule count, so these profiles do not isolate proof-depth effects. The two renderers express each rule either as If and b, then or as holds whenever and hold. Rule order stays fixed. The model and competence criterion are unchanged: both answers must be correct. The same (R, D, ) profile, invariance, and chance correction apply. Thus adoption requires task-specific latent instances, an oracle, and semantics-preserving renderers, without changing the outcome decomposition or analysis. This demonstrates second instantiation; it does not measure implementation effort or imply that arbitrary presentation equivalence can be certified automatically. C.

sections.title: Analysis
sections.content: G.1 Training-Seed Replication The main text reports seed 42, selected for higher mean invariance on the twelve clean held-out relations. This selection uses the reported held-out evaluation results. Seed 43 uses the same training and evaluation recipe. Table 19 retains both runs, including their front/behind results, and Figure 9 resolves their profiles by chain length. The selected run is not uniformly stronger on every metric: seed 43 has higher mean accuracy and κ across the twelve relations. Both runs retain substantial long-chain failures. Why the agreement bonus was inert. The nominal reward of the GRPO runs in Section 6 is = correct + λ max(0, agree chance) with λ = 1/2, where agree is the share of samples on the instances other presentations that give the same answer and chance = q2 + (1 q)2 with the instances yes-rate. Each batch holds the four presentations of one instance (original, equivalent, reshuffled, fully rewritten) times = 4 samples, but the trainer forms the advantage group per prompt, that is per presentation. Within one group the other presentations answers, and chance are shared by all four samples, and every answer is yes or no (no run produced an unparsed answer), so the reward takes two values, one for the gold answer and one for the other. The agreement term shifts the gap between them by at most λ/2 = 0.25 and cannot reverse it, since the correctness gap is 1, and with group-normalized advantages (r mean)/std of two-valued group depend only on how many of the four samples were right, not on the size of the gap. Hence λ = 1/2 and λ = 0 give the same 26 advantages (up to the 104 added to the standard deviation), and the logged cosine between the advantage vector used and the λ = 0 vector is 1.0000 on every step with nonzero advantage. The signal was also sparse: step has nonzero advantage only if some presentations four samples disagree, which happened on 28 of 600 steps for GRPO seed 42 and 31 of 600 for seed 43, and the gradient is zero on every other step. The transfer in Section 6 is the effect of these few correctness updates, not of an agreement term. variant in which the bonus can act. Rescaling the reward is not enough: the policy gradient is linear in the advantages and every nonzero GRPO step had gradient norm of 238 against clipping maximum of 1, so bonus matters only if it changes the direction of the advantage vector. That requires all presentations of an instance to share one advantage group and the instances rewards to take three or more values. The grpo-ig variant groups all sixteen samples of an instance, uses the instances mean reward as the baseline without group scaling, and rewards correct + λ(agree chance) without the clip at zero; everything else follows the GRPO recipe (the same 19 held-in relations, 600 instances, = 16 to 128, = 4). We trained λ = 0 and λ = 0.5 with seeds 42 and 43. Each λ = 0.5 run had 3234 of 600 steps with nonzero advantage, and the bonus changed the update direction on 30 of them, with mean cosine of 0.9987 to the λ = 0 vector, about 3: with yes/no answers and gold label shared by all presentations, the majority answer of an informative instance is almost always the gold one, so rewarding agreement points the same way as rewarding correctness. Identical-Prompt Repeat Agreement H.1 Control and Interpretation We estimate identical-prompt repeat agreement by sending each original prompt to the same model again under the same decoding settings and comparing the two answers. This measures run-to-run agreement without changing the prompt. We contrast it with invariance between the original and an equivalent presentation. Both agreement measures condition on parseable answers in the corresponding pair. Earlier tables call this control the re-sampling floor or self-agreement. It is measured reference, not universal lower bound. Cross-presentation agreement below it indicates sensitivity beyond the observed original-prompt repeat level. The difference does not causally isolate presentation error, since answer uncertainty can differ between presentations. It also does not establish competence ranking by itself. Repeated sampling of both presentations would provide stronger characterization of decoding variability. H.2 Base Ordering Models On front/behind, identical-prompt agreement ranges from 64.8% to 96.4% across the six base models.
